title: Vibe Coding 04 — Debugging, Review & Product Quality
description: Investigate root causes, independently review generated diffs, evaluate dependencies, measure real-world performance, and build inclusive internationalized interfaces. Part 4 of 5.

paths.title: Debugging & Root-Cause Analysis
paths.description: Diagnose defects with evidence, reproducibility, and causal reasoning instead of prompting the model to make random patches.

paths.title: Code Review & AI Review
paths.description: Review generated changes for behavior, architecture, security, maintainability, and evidence rather than accepting plausible-looking code.

paths.title: Dependencies & Package Hygiene
paths.description: Choose, verify, update, and remove third-party packages safely when coding agents can suggest libraries faster than humans can assess them.

paths.title: Performance & Scalability
paths.description: Keep AI-generated software responsive and efficient by measuring bottlenecks, setting budgets, and optimizing the right layer.

paths.title: Accessibility & Internationalization
paths.description: Ensure generated products work for diverse users, input methods, languages, locales, and content lengths.

cards.title: Reproduce before fixing
cards.prompt: What is an evidence-led sequence for reproducing a reported bug?
cards.content: A reliable reproduction defines the actual problem. Capture exact inputs, environment, steps, expected behavior, and observed behavior.
steps: Capture the expected and observed behavior with exact environment/version.
Collect the smallest input and steps that reliably trigger the failure.
Record logs, stack traces, relevant persistence state, and timing.
Confirm the failure on the current head before modifying code.
Turn the reproduction into a focused regression check.

cards.title: Reduce the failing case
cards.prompt: How can reducing a failing input help isolate the responsible component?
cards.content: Smaller reproductions reveal which variables matter. Remove unrelated data, components, or steps while preserving the failure.

cards.title: Read the error literally
cards.prompt: Why should the exact first error be inspected rather than guessed around?
cards.content: Stack traces and diagnostics often identify the failing boundary. Start from the first relevant error and trace data and control flow around it.

cards.title: Distinguish symptom from cause
cards.prompt: A save button shows a spinner forever because a rejected promise never clears loading state. What is the underlying defect?

options: Extend the network timeout to give the save more time.
The failed async path does not perform state cleanup.
Debounce clicks to prevent duplicate saves without observing rejection handling.
Clear loading state after an arbitrary timer independent of operation completion.
question.explanation: Visible failures may originate far upstream. Ask what invariant became false first rather than patching the last line that crashed. Fix and test the missing failure-path cleanup rather than masking its visual symptom.

cards.title: Compare working and failing states
cards.prompt: Which differences between a passing and failing environment offer useful evidence?
cards.content: Differences narrow the search space. Compare environment, inputs, versions, flags, permissions, and recent commits.

cards.title: Use logs with correlation
cards.prompt: How can correlated logs reconstruct the sequence leading to a failed request?
cards.content: Distributed failures need a thread across components. Preserve request, job, or user-safe correlation identifiers through logs and traces.

cards.title: Inspect actual runtime values
cards.prompt: Why is inspecting actual values more reliable than trusting a model's assumed state?
cards.content: Model reasoning about hypothetical values is weaker than evidence. Use debugger, structured logs, assertions, or temporary instrumentation to inspect state.

cards.title: Bisect regressions
cards.prompt: The git bisect commands mark one known bad and one known good revision. How does repeated midpoint testing isolate the regression?
cards.content: When a bug appeared after a known good version, history is evidence. Use commit bisection or controlled rollback to find the first bad change.

code.snippet:
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v1.8.0
# test each midpoint until the first bad commit is isolated

cards.title: Check environmental drift
cards.prompt: What runtime, configuration, or dependency drift can explain environment-specific failures?
cards.content: Builds can fail because runtime and local assumptions differ. Compare environment variables, versions, platform, filesystem, network, and data state.

cards.title: Check race conditions
cards.prompt: Which ordering-dependent bug could disappear during single-request testing?
cards.content: Intermittent failures often depend on timing. Look for shared mutable state, missing awaits, duplicate events, stale reads, and unsafe retries.

cards.title: Check caches
cards.prompt: How can stale caches conceal an otherwise correct code change?
cards.content: Stale state can make new code appear broken. Identify browser, CDN, application, build, database, and service-worker caches in the path.

cards.title: Check serialization boundaries
cards.prompt: Where can encoding, JSON parsing, or type conversion corrupt data across an interface?
cards.content: Data can change shape across JSON, dates, numbers, and nullable fields. Inspect encoded and decoded representations at each boundary.

cards.title: Check permissions and identity
cards.prompt: Which user and tenant identities must be checked when an action unexpectedly fails?
cards.content: Many apparent not-found or server errors are authorization problems. Inspect the authenticated identity, scopes, ownership, and policy decisions.

cards.title: Check database state
cards.prompt: What database records or transaction state might explain inconsistent application output?
cards.content: Schema and data invariants may differ from assumptions. Inspect migrations, constraints, representative rows, locks, and query plans.

cards.title: Avoid shotgun fixes
cards.prompt: Why can changing several likely causes at once make debugging slower?
cards.content: Changing many plausible causes at once destroys diagnostic information. Test one hypothesis at a time or isolate changes so cause remains attributable.

cards.title: Use temporary assertions
cards.prompt: When should temporary assertions be added to expose a violated invariant?
cards.content: Assertions can expose the first violated invariant closer to its source. Add targeted checks during investigation and remove or formalize them after the fix.

cards.title: Turn the bug into a test
cards.prompt: What must a regression test establish after a defect is fixed?
cards.content: A regression test prevents recurrence and proves the fix addresses the observed case. Write the failing test before or alongside the correction when feasible.
items: It reproduces the original failure before the repair.
Its assertion protects user-visible behavior or an authoritative invariant.
It passes only when the causal defect is corrected, not when checks are weakened.
At least one adjacent success or failure path remains intact.
The test runs in the appropriate CI layer.

cards.title: Validate adjacent behavior
cards.prompt: What nearby user behavior might a narrowly successful fix still break?
cards.content: A narrow bug fix can break neighboring cases. Test both the reproduction and nearby valid scenarios.

cards.title: Remove diagnostic noise
cards.prompt: Which debug logs and temporary workarounds should be removed before merging?
cards.content: Temporary logs and flags can leak data or clutter production. Clean up investigation artifacts before merge unless they provide durable observability.

cards.title: Write the root cause
cards.prompt: What should a root-cause report distinguish from mere remediation steps?
cards.content: A concise causal explanation improves future prevention. Document trigger, violated assumption, why existing checks missed it, fix, and prevention.

cards.title: Review intent before syntax
cards.prompt: Why should a reviewer establish the requested change before reading the diff line by line?
cards.content: Correct-looking code can implement the wrong requirement. Start by comparing the diff to the task and acceptance criteria.

cards.title: Review behavior-changing lines first
cards.prompt: Which lines deserve attention first because they change observable behavior or permissions?
cards.content: Formatting noise should not consume the same attention as logic. Prioritize control flow, state changes, queries, permissions, network calls, and persistence.

cards.title: Trace data flow
cards.prompt: How do you trace a behavior-changing data flow during a code review?
cards.content: Security and correctness issues often cross file boundaries. Follow important inputs from entry through validation, transformation, storage, and output.
steps: Identify the entry point and which fields are untrusted.
Follow parsing and validation into policy or permission checks.
Trace authoritative writes, transactions, and downstream side effects.
Inspect error, retry, and serialization paths.
Compare the observed behavior with acceptance criteria and focused tests.

cards.title: Check authorization at the server
cards.prompt: Why must a security reviewer check authorization where the server enforces it?
cards.content: Client-side hiding is not an access-control mechanism. Verify every sensitive operation enforces permissions in trusted code.

cards.title: Check error handling
cards.prompt: Which failure and retry paths should a code reviewer trace?
cards.content: Generated code often under-specifies failure behavior. Look for swallowed errors, broad catches, fail-open logic, missing rollback, and unusable messages.

cards.title: Check async behavior
cards.prompt: What can happen if a handler reports success before an asynchronous write commits?
cards.content: Missing awaits and stale closures create subtle defects. Inspect concurrency, cancellation, retries, cleanup, and race-prone state.

cards.title: Check dependency changes
cards.prompt: What should a reviewer investigate when a patch adds or upgrades a dependency?
cards.content: A one-line import can pull significant risk. Verify package identity, necessity, version, license, and maintenance.

cards.title: Check duplicated logic
cards.prompt: How can duplicated business logic create contradictory behavior over time?
cards.content: AI may solve locally by copying an existing pattern imperfectly. Search for authoritative existing utilities or services before accepting duplication.

cards.title: Check architectural boundaries
cards.prompt: Which proposed changes violate established module ownership or dependency direction?
cards.content: A feature can work while making the system harder to evolve. Look for new cross-layer imports, cycles, global state, or database access in inappropriate layers.

cards.title: Check types and schemas
cards.prompt: Why must type assertions and schema changes be checked against actual runtime data?
cards.content: Type escape hatches can hide contract errors. Scrutinize casts, any-like types, ignored errors, optionality, and schema mismatches.

cards.title: Check tests for false confidence
cards.prompt: How can a passing test suite give false confidence in generated code?
cards.content: Tests can mirror the implementation and miss the real contract. Ensure tests cover acceptance, failure, permissions, and realistic integration.

cards.title: Check accessibility
cards.prompt: Which keyboard, focus, and accessible-name changes might a visual diff overlook?
cards.content: Visual review alone misses interaction defects. Inspect semantics, focus, keyboard behavior, labels, and state announcements.

cards.title: Check performance impact
cards.prompt: What workload or query consequences might accompany a seemingly small code change?
cards.content: Generated loops and queries can scale badly. Look for repeated work, N+1 requests, unbounded lists, heavy client bundles, and missing caching rationale.

cards.title: Check observability
cards.prompt: Which missing logs or identifiers would make a new production failure hard to diagnose?
cards.content: New critical behavior should be diagnosable. Verify safe logs, metrics, traces, or audit events for important operations.

cards.title: Use AI as a second reviewer
cards.prompt: How can a second AI reviewer contribute without replacing independent evidence?
cards.content: An independent model can surface issues the authoring model missed. Ask a reviewer agent to inspect the diff adversarially with the spec and repository instructions.

cards.title: Do not treat AI review as approval
cards.prompt: An independent AI reviewer says a PR is safe, but the authorization path is untested. How should a maintainer respond?

options: Ask another model for a favorable review and treat agreement as validation.
Merge when CI passes even if no test exercises resource-level permissions.
Treat the approval as a hypothesis and require a concrete authorization check and current-head evidence.
Defer testing the authorization path until after release and rely on monitoring.
question.explanation: Automated review is fallible and context-limited. Validate AI findings and retain human ownership for consequential merges. An attributed reviewer opinion does not replace execution, traceability, or human accountability.

cards.title: Review generated configuration carefully
cards.prompt: Which generated configuration files require special security and environment scrutiny?
cards.content: CI, infrastructure, permissions, and deployment files can create broad effects. Inspect every privilege, secret reference, trigger, environment, and destructive command.

cards.title: Review deletions and renamed behavior
cards.prompt: How can deleted code or renamed behavior introduce regression beyond obvious additions?
cards.content: AI can remove code it believes is unused. Confirm callers, compatibility, migrations, and feature flags before accepting removal.

cards.title: Review the final head
cards.prompt: This shell sequence inspects diff statistics, relevant files, tests, and type checks. What additional verification is needed when the head changes?
cards.content: Earlier review does not cover later fixes. Perform a final diff and check review after all requested changes are applied.

code.snippet:
git diff --stat main...HEAD
git diff main...HEAD -- src/ test/
npm test
npm run typecheck

cards.title: Write review conclusions
cards.prompt: What makes a final PR-review conclusion actionable?
cards.content: High-value review records why the change is acceptable. Summarize tested behavior, remaining risks, follow-ups, and any consciously accepted tradeoffs.
items: State which requirements were and were not verified.
Identify the reviewed commit and relevant files or symbols.
Report concrete test results, not only a mergeable flag.
Explain unresolved security, persistence, performance, or UX risks.
Name the exact changes or evidence needed before merge.

cards.title: Prefer the standard platform
cards.prompt: When does a standard library or platform feature remove the need for an extra package?
cards.content: Every dependency adds supply-chain and maintenance cost. Use built-in language or framework capabilities when they solve the requirement cleanly.

cards.title: Verify package identity
cards.prompt: What can npm view and the lockfile diff establish about an AI-proposed dependency, and what do they NOT prove?
cards.content: Models can hallucinate packages or suggest lookalikes. Check the official registry, publisher, repository, documentation, and package name before installing. npm view provides registry metadata for the named package, while the lockfile diff shows resolved version and dependency-tree changes. Neither proves the package is benign, maintained, API-compatible, or safe to install without further review.

code.snippet:
npm view zod name version repository license
npm audit --omit=dev
git diff -- package.json package-lock.json

cards.title: Assess maintenance health
cards.prompt: What indicators reveal whether a dependency has a credible maintenance history?
cards.content: Popularity alone does not guarantee sustainability. Review release recency, issue activity, supported runtimes, maintainers, and deprecation notices.

cards.title: Check licensing
cards.prompt: Before adopting a third-party dependency, what licensing questions must be checked?
cards.content: A technically suitable package may be legally incompatible. Review license terms and organization policy before adoption.
items: The package and major transitive licenses are identified.
Distribution, attribution, modification, and source obligations are understood.
The intended commercial or open-source use is permitted.
Vendored binaries or assets have appropriate usage rights.
A reviewer can trace the decision and current dependency version.

cards.title: Pin reproducibly
cards.prompt: How do lockfiles and pinned versions support repeatable installs?
cards.content: Floating versions make builds change without source changes. Use lockfiles and appropriate version constraints; pin critical build inputs more tightly.

cards.title: Review lockfile diffs
cards.prompt: Why should a reviewer inspect lockfile changes rather than only package.json?
cards.content: Transitive changes may be larger than the requested package. Inspect added packages, unexpected upgrades, registries, and integrity metadata.

cards.title: Minimize dependency surface
cards.prompt: How does an unnecessary dependency increase security and support obligations?
cards.content: Convenience libraries can introduce large trees for small features. Compare package cost with implementing a small, well-understood utility.

cards.title: Separate dev and runtime dependencies
cards.prompt: Which packages truly belong in runtime rather than development dependencies?
cards.content: Production should not ship tooling it does not need. Classify packages by where they execute and build artifacts accordingly.

cards.title: Use trusted registries
cards.prompt: Why does the identity of a package registry matter to build trust?
cards.content: Registry configuration controls what code can enter builds. Restrict package sources and authenticate private registries securely.

cards.title: Protect install scripts
cards.prompt: An unknown package requests a postinstall script that downloads and runs a remote binary. What is the appropriate response?

options: Review provenance and script behavior before allowing installation in a privileged environment.
Pin the exact version but otherwise allow its postinstall script to execute unchecked.
Rely only on a vulnerability scanner to assess the remote command.
Run installation in production CI because a public registry already accepted the package.
question.explanation: Package lifecycle scripts can execute arbitrary code. Understand package trust and consider safer install policies in sensitive environments. Installation hooks execute code and therefore deserve supply-chain review.

cards.title: Scan known vulnerabilities
cards.prompt: How should a known vulnerability report be evaluated in application context?
cards.content: Dependency risk changes after merge. Use automated advisory or dependency scanning and triage findings by exploitability and exposure.

cards.title: Update incrementally
cards.prompt: What is a safe procedure for updating a significant dependency?
cards.content: Large version jumps combine many behavioral changes. Read migration notes and update in manageable steps with tests.
steps: Read changelogs, supported versions, security advisories, and migration notes.
Upgrade one coherent package group and preserve the lockfile.
Inspect transitive and install-script changes.
Run unit, contract, build, and relevant runtime compatibility tests.
Stage or release with monitoring and a versioned rollback option.

cards.title: Avoid abandoned packages
cards.prompt: What risks appear when a foundational package is no longer maintained?
cards.content: Unmaintained code accumulates compatibility and security risk. Replace critical abandoned dependencies before they become blockers.

cards.title: Remove unused packages
cards.prompt: How can unused-package removal reduce attack surface and deployment size?
cards.content: Dead dependencies remain supply-chain and build liabilities. Periodically detect and remove packages no longer imported or required.

cards.title: Control transitive overrides carefully
cards.prompt: When might a transitive version override fix one issue but break another package?
cards.content: Forced resolutions can create unsupported combinations. Document why overrides exist and remove them when upstream fixes arrive.

cards.title: Verify binary and native packages
cards.prompt: What platform and build implications accompany native or binary packages?
cards.content: Prebuilt artifacts increase platform and provenance considerations. Check supported architectures, signatures or provenance, and fallback build requirements.

cards.title: Review SDK permissions
cards.prompt: Which user or cloud permissions should be examined before adding an SDK?
cards.content: Cloud and third-party SDKs can expose powerful APIs. Use least-privilege credentials and configure only required capabilities.

cards.title: Track breaking changes
cards.prompt: How should breaking release notes influence an upgrade plan?
cards.content: Agent-generated upgrades may compile while subtly changing semantics. Read changelogs for auth, defaults, serialization, caching, and error behavior.

cards.title: Automate dependency policy
cards.prompt: Which repository checks can consistently enforce acceptable dependency choices?
cards.content: Manual review alone does not scale. Use bots, scanners, allowlists, and required checks appropriate to repository risk.

cards.title: Document major dependency choices
cards.prompt: What reasons for adopting a major dependency should be written down?
cards.content: Frameworks and core libraries shape architecture for years. Record why major packages were selected, alternatives considered, and exit considerations.

cards.title: Measure before optimizing
cards.prompt: How should a team investigate and improve a performance complaint?
cards.content: Intuition is unreliable about real bottlenecks. Profile latency, CPU, memory, network, queries, and rendering before changing architecture.
steps: Define an affected user journey and measurable baseline.
Capture traces or profiles under representative input and load.
Find the dominant latency, CPU, memory, network, or query contributor.
Make one bounded optimization with explicit trade-offs.
Repeat the measurement and compare relevant tail latencies and regressions.

cards.title: Set performance budgets
cards.prompt: How can explicit latency and bundle-size budgets make performance testable?
cards.content: Without thresholds, regressions accumulate gradually. Define budgets for key user and server metrics and enforce them where practical.

cards.title: Optimize user-perceived latency
cards.prompt: What is the difference between server throughput and perceived user responsiveness?
cards.content: Backend speed alone does not determine experience. Measure time to useful content, interaction responsiveness, and completion of important actions.

cards.title: Avoid unbounded work
cards.prompt: What should bound the size and duration of a data-processing operation?
cards.content: Lists, loops, searches, and uploads can grow beyond expected sizes. Paginate, cap, stream, or batch work based on realistic limits.

cards.title: Prevent N+1 queries
cards.prompt: How can per-item database fetching cause N+1 query amplification?
cards.content: Repeated data access is a common generated-code scaling defect. Inspect query count per request and batch related data.

cards.title: Use indexes from workload evidence
cards.prompt: In EXPLAIN ANALYZE for this limited, ordered query, which plan details reveal whether an index matches the workload?
cards.content: Indexes speed reads but cost writes and storage. Create indexes around real filter, join, and ordering patterns and verify query plans.

code.snippet:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT p.id, p.title
FROM project p
WHERE p.workspace_id = $1
ORDER BY p.updated_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

cards.title: Cache with an invalidation model
cards.prompt: A cache makes project reads fast but users now receive obsolete permissions. What design element is missing?

options: Increase cache lifetime to reduce database load further.
Monitor cache hit rate without considering permission freshness.
Attach a client ETag without revisiting the server's authorization-cache lifecycle.
An invalidation or expiry rule that preserves the authorization invariant.
question.explanation: Caching without freshness rules creates correctness bugs. Define cache key, owner, lifetime, invalidation, and fallback before adding a cache. Caching correctness includes when stale data must stop being served, especially for permissions.

cards.title: Compress and minimize payloads
cards.prompt: When are compression and smaller response payloads worth prioritizing?
cards.content: Sending unnecessary data wastes bandwidth and parsing time. Select needed fields, paginate results, compress responses, and avoid oversized JSON.

cards.title: Control client bundle growth
cards.prompt: How can dependency or component growth increase initial JavaScript costs?
cards.content: AI can import large libraries for small UI needs. Track bundles and prefer selective imports, code splitting, and platform features.

cards.title: Optimize images and media
cards.prompt: What media delivery choices reduce unnecessary network and rendering work?
cards.content: Large media often dominates page weight. Serve appropriately sized formats, responsive sources, lazy load noncritical content, and reserve dimensions.

cards.title: Avoid blocking the main thread
cards.prompt: Why can synchronous browser work make an otherwise fast endpoint feel slow?
cards.content: Long JavaScript tasks make interfaces feel frozen. Split heavy work, use workers when justified, and minimize synchronous computation during interaction.

cards.title: Use concurrency deliberately
cards.prompt: When does extra concurrency improve throughput, and when does it overload dependencies?
cards.content: Parallel work helps only when dependencies and limits permit it. Bound concurrency to protect databases, APIs, memory, and rate limits.

cards.title: Use backpressure
cards.prompt: How does backpressure protect a slow downstream consumer?
cards.content: Producers can overwhelm slower consumers. Apply queue limits, streaming flow control, or admission limits under load.

cards.title: Load test critical paths
cards.prompt: What workload distribution should a meaningful load test represent?
cards.content: Unit performance does not predict whole-system contention. Test representative traffic, concurrency, data size, and failure conditions.

cards.title: Profile memory
cards.prompt: How can retaining objects accidentally grow a long-running process's memory?
cards.content: Leaks and retained data can crash long-running processes. Inspect heap growth, caches, subscriptions, listeners, and unbounded collections.

cards.title: Design autoscaling signals
cards.prompt: Which measured signal should trigger autoscaling instead of guesswork?
cards.content: CPU alone may not reflect workload pressure. Scale on metrics related to queue depth, concurrency, latency, or resource saturation.

cards.title: Protect dependencies under load
cards.prompt: What limits prevent upstream spikes from exhausting shared dependencies?
cards.content: Scaling the frontend tier can overload databases or third parties. Use connection limits, rate controls, caching, queues, and circuit behavior.

cards.title: Test cold starts and warmup
cards.prompt: Why should deployment validation include cold-start or warmup behavior when relevant?
cards.content: Serverless and container workloads can behave differently after idle periods. Measure initialization and reduce heavy startup or provide capacity where latency matters.

cards.title: Observe tail latency
cards.prompt: What should a latency report include beyond the average?
cards.content: Averages can hide severe slow experiences. Track percentiles such as p95 or p99 for important operations.
items: p95/p99 response or interaction latency is tracked for critical routes.
Sample volume and load characteristics are stated.
Cold-start and dependency-failure periods are not silently excluded.
Changes are compared to an equivalent baseline and budget.
User-relevant effects accompany server-level measurements.

cards.title: Re-measure after optimization
cards.prompt: How should engineers verify that an optimization improves the original bottleneck?
cards.content: An optimization is only successful if evidence improves without unacceptable tradeoffs. Compare before and after metrics and watch for correctness, cost, or complexity regressions.

cards.title: Use semantic structure
cards.prompt: Why should generated interfaces start with meaningful HTML structure?
cards.content: Assistive technology depends on meaningful markup. Use headings, landmarks, lists, tables, labels, and native controls according to purpose.

cards.title: Provide accessible names
cards.prompt: What makes a visible icon control discoverable to a screen reader?
cards.content: Icon-only controls are ambiguous without text alternatives. Ensure interactive elements have meaningful visible labels or accessible names.

cards.title: Maintain visible focus
cards.prompt: How should visible focus help keyboard users locate their next action?
cards.content: Keyboard users need to know where interaction is occurring. Use clear focus indicators with adequate contrast and never remove focus without replacement.

cards.title: Support complete keyboard operation
cards.prompt: A menu opens on hover but has no keyboard trigger or visible focus. Which requirement remains unmet?

options: Set tabindex=0 on the hover menu without adding keyboard activation.
The entire journey must be operable by keyboard with perceivable focus.
Add focus styling but keep activation dependent on pointer hover.
Support Escape to dismiss the menu without making it keyboard-openable.
question.explanation: Every pointer interaction should have a keyboard path. Test tab order, activation, escape, arrow-key patterns, and no keyboard traps. A visually interactive control must still support non-pointer users.

cards.title: Manage dialog focus
cards.prompt: What is correct focus management for a modal dialog?
cards.content: Modal interfaces require predictable focus containment and restoration. Move focus into dialogs, trap appropriately, and restore to the invoking control on close.
steps: Trigger the dialog from a labeled, keyboard-operable control.
On open, move focus to a sensible element within the dialog.
Keep keyboard focus within the modal while it is active.
Support Escape and a visible close action where appropriate.
On close, return focus to the invoking control or a logical fallback.

cards.title: Announce dynamic updates
cards.prompt: How should a live-region update announce status without becoming noisy?
cards.content: Screen-reader users may not notice visual state changes. Use appropriate live regions or status semantics for important asynchronous feedback.

cards.title: Meet contrast requirements
cards.prompt: Why must text, controls, and focus indicators retain sufficient contrast?
cards.content: Muted AI-generated palettes can become unreadable. Measure text, icon, control, and focus contrast instead of judging by appearance.

cards.title: Support zoom and text resizing
cards.prompt: What layouts fail when users zoom or increase the default text size?
cards.content: Fixed layouts can break when users enlarge content. Allow reflow and avoid clipping at high zoom or larger text settings.

cards.title: Respect motion preferences
cards.prompt: How should animation and scrolling respond to reduced-motion preferences?
cards.content: Animation can cause discomfort or distract from tasks. Reduce or remove nonessential motion when the user requests reduced motion.

cards.title: Provide text alternatives
cards.prompt: What information must an image's alternative text communicate in context?
cards.content: Images and charts need equivalent meaning. Write concise alt text or nearby descriptions based on the image's purpose.

cards.title: Use accessible form errors
cards.prompt: In the labeled email field, how do for/id and aria-describedby connect the control to its name and an error message?
cards.content: Color alone is not a sufficient error signal. Associate clear error text with the relevant field and focus or summarize errors appropriately.

cards.title: Test with assistive technology
cards.prompt: What manual assistive-technology checks complement automated accessibility scanners?
cards.content: Automated scanners do not cover all usability. Perform keyboard and representative screen-reader testing on critical flows.

cards.title: Externalize user-facing strings
cards.prompt: Why should user-visible copy be externalized rather than scattered through components?
cards.content: Hard-coded strings block translation workflows. Keep translatable content separate from code and avoid string concatenation that assumes word order.

cards.title: Design for text expansion
cards.prompt: How can translated labels change button widths and navigation layouts?
cards.content: Translations can be substantially longer than source text. Use flexible layouts and test long labels, buttons, and navigation.

cards.title: Use locale-aware formatting
cards.prompt: Why should dates, numbers, currencies, and times follow user locale and timezone?
cards.content: Dates, numbers, currencies, and plural rules differ by locale. Use internationalization APIs and explicit locale or time-zone handling.

cards.title: Avoid encoding meaning in color only
cards.prompt: How can an interface convey status without depending solely on red versus green?
cards.content: Color perception varies and assistive technology may not convey color. Combine color with text, icons, patterns, or position.

cards.title: Support right-to-left layout when required
cards.prompt: When might a right-to-left language require changes to visual order and icons?
cards.content: RTL languages affect alignment, order, and directional icons. Use logical CSS properties and test mirrored layouts.

cards.title: Localize validation thoughtfully
cards.prompt: What contextual information must localized validation messages preserve?
cards.content: Input formats and names vary across cultures. Avoid assumptions about postal codes, names, phone numbers, and date entry beyond business requirements. A localized validation message should retain the field name, violated rule, locale-appropriate expected format or limit, and an actionable correction; translation must not silently alter the underlying business constraint.

cards.title: Include accessibility in acceptance criteria
cards.prompt: Which accessibility requirements should be included in a feature's acceptance criteria?
cards.content: Accessibility work is missed when treated as optional polish. Specify keyboard, focus, semantics, contrast, and announcements in the feature definition.
items: Semantic controls have discernible names, roles, and states.
The primary journey is keyboard-operable with visible focus.
Forms expose labels, validation errors, and status announcements.
Text zoom, contrast, motion preference, and mobile reflow are supported.
Automated checks and relevant manual assistive-technology flows are recorded.

cards.title: Prevent regression with automation
cards.prompt: How can accessibility tests prevent later AI-generated changes from undoing good behavior?
cards.content: Accessibility needs continuous protection. Add linting and automated checks while retaining manual verification for critical interactions.
